stem: Increasing the carbon content of ordinary steel generally decreases its:
reason: More carbon → harder and stronger steel but less ductile and harder to weld.

stem: Seasoning of timber is the process of:
reason: Seasoning removes sap/moisture to ≈ 12–15 % → strength, durability, less warping.

stem: The property by which a material regains its original shape after removal of load is:
reason: Elasticity = full recovery on unloading; plasticity = permanent deformation.

stem: Lime used in lime mortar for masonry:
reason: Fat lime → plaster/whitewash. · Depends on: hydraulic lime is best for masonry (esp. damp places); fat lime can also be used.

stem: The depression provided on the top face of a brick is called a:
reason: Frog (10–20 mm deep) is laid upward so mortar fills it and keys the courses; closers and bats are cut bricks.

stem: Plaster of Paris is obtained by the partial dehydration of which material?
reason: Gypsum $\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot 2H_2O}$ heated to ≈ 150–170 °C loses $1\tfrac{1}{2}$ $\mathrm{H_2O}$ → $\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot \tfrac{1}{2}H_2O}$ (Plaster of Paris).

stem: Lacquer is commonly described in elementary building-material questions as:
reason: Lacquer = spirit varnish (resin dissolved in spirit), quick-drying and glossy.

stem: Quartzite consists predominantly of:
reason: Quartzite = metamorphosed sandstone, mainly quartz (siliceous).

stem: Silica in suitable proportions in brick earth mainly helps to:

options.C: Make the brick soluble in water

reason: Silica (50–60 %) prevents shrinkage, cracking and warping; alumina gives plasticity.

stem: The cement compound primarily responsible for early strength is:
reason: $\mathrm{C_3S}$ → early (1–7 day) strength; $\mathrm{C_2S}$ → later strength; $\mathrm{C_3A}$ → flash set and highest heat.

stem: Timber is generally strongest in tension or compression when the load acts:
reason: Fibres are aligned along the grain, so timber is strongest parallel to it.

stem: Which is the primary lime-bearing raw material used to manufacture ordinary Portland cement?
reason: Limestone (calcareous) supplies the lime; clay/shale (argillaceous) supplies silica and alumina.

stem: Which metallic element is present in the greatest proportion in ordinary Portland cement?
reason: Lime (CaO ≈ 60–67 %) is the largest constituent, so calcium is the most abundant metal.

stem: Excess silica in brick earth primarily causes:

options.D: Loss of cohesion and brittle bricks

reason: Excess silica destroys cohesion, making bricks brittle and weak.

stem: What generally happens to cement strength after prolonged storage in ordinary conditions?
reason: Cement absorbs moisture in storage: ≈ 20 % strength loss in 3 months, 40 % in a year.

stem: Which cement is commonly used for decorative cement paint?
reason: White cement (iron-free) is the base of decorative cement paints and terrazzo.

stem: Le Chatelier’s apparatus is used to determine cement:
reason: Le Chatelier apparatus → soundness (free-lime expansion ≤ 10 mm); autoclave test → MgO.

stem: What is the minimum initial setting time of ordinary Portland cement?
reason: OPC initial setting ≥ 30 min; final ≤ 600 min (IS 269/4031).

stem: Bulking of coarse aggregate is generally:
reason: Moisture films are thin compared with coarse particles, so coarse aggregate hardly bulks; fine sand bulks 20–40 %.

stem: Bulking of sand means:

options.D: An increase in volume due to moisture

reason: Bulking = volume increase of damp sand (max at 4–6 % moisture); dry and saturated sand show none.

stem: Which apparatus is used to determine standard consistency and setting time of cement?
reason: Vicat apparatus: 10 mm plunger for consistency, needle for initial and collar for final setting.

stem: What is the maximum final setting time of ordinary Portland cement?
reason: OPC final setting time ≤ 600 min (10 h).

stem: Maximum water absorption of 1st-class brick (NEC key):
reason: Best pick (high confidence): NBC 109:1994 cl. 3.4.1: a first-class brick may absorb at most 15% water after 24 h immersion (the clause allows up to 25% for some handmade bricks). Nepal code wins here. · Switch: if IS 1077 strength classes are used: class ≤ 12.5 → 20%, higher classes → 15%.

stem: How does ductility change as the percentage reduction in area in a tensile test increases?
reason: % reduction in area and % elongation measure ductility: the larger they are, the more ductile the steel.

stem: In the traditional first-class building-brick classification, the minimum compressive strength is approximately:
reason: First-class brick ≥ 10.5 N/mm²; second class 7; third class 3.5 N/mm².

stem: A sanded cement grout is a mixture of:
reason: Sanded grout = cement + sand + water; neat cement grout = cement + water only.

stem: Before plastering, a smooth concrete surface should be made:
reason: A smooth surface is hacked/roughened to give the plaster a mechanical key.

stem: For a straight flight between two landings, the number of treads is generally:

options.A: One less than the number of risers
options.B: Equal to the number of risers
options.C: One more than the number of risers

reason: Treads = risers − 1 (the top riser lands on the floor/landing).

stem: A projecting masonry or concrete bracket supporting a beam or truss is a:
reason: Corbel = projecting masonry/concrete that supports a beam or truss.

stem: The lowest projecting edge of a sloping roof is the:
reason: Eaves = lowest overhanging edge of a sloping roof; ridge = the top apex line.

stem: Why are dry clay bricks soaked before laying in cement mortar?

options.B: To reduce absorption of water from mortar

reason: Main reason is B (dry bricks suck water from mortar); with every option true here, pick ‘all of the above’.
note: If “all of the above” is not offered, mark B.

stem: Under IS 456 normal conditions with ordinary Portland cement, vertical formwork to columns and walls can generally be removed after:
reason: IS 456: vertical faces of columns, walls, beams 16–24 h; slab soffit 3 days; beam soffit 7 days.

stem: For many repetitions of the same concrete formwork, which material is generally preferred for durability and reuse?
reason: Steel forms are durable and give the most reuses; timber suits few repetitions.

stem: The elastic section modulus of a solid circular section of diameter $d$ is:
The second moment of area of a solid circle of diameter $d$ about a centroidal diameter is:
reason: Solid circle about a diameter: $\pi d^{4}/64$; polar moment $\pi d^{4}/32$.

stem: The centre of gravity of a solid hemisphere lies at what distance from its flat face?
reason: Solid hemisphere $3r/8$ from the flat face; hemispherical shell $r/2$; semicircular area $4r/3\pi$.

stem: For a hollow circular section with outer diameter $D$ and inner diameter $d$, the second moment of area about a centroidal diameter is:
reason: Hollow circle $I = \pi(D^{4} - d^{4})/64$; divide by $D/2$ for the section modulus.

stem: For a uniform solid cone of height $h$, its centre of gravity lies above the base by:
reason: Solid cone CG at $h/4$ from the base; hollow cone (surface) $h/3$.

stem: A trapezoidal area has parallel sides $a$ at the top and $b$ at the base, separated by height $h$. Its centroid measured from base $b$ is:
reason: Centroid from the longer base $b$: $h(b + 2a)/[3(a + b)]$.

stem: The elastic section modulus of a hollow circular section, outer diameter $D$ and inner diameter $d$, is:
reason: $Z = I/(D/2) = \pi(D^{4} - d^{4})/(32D)$ — always divide by the outer diameter.

stem: The second moment of area of a rectangle of width $b$ and depth $d$ about its base is:
reason: About the base $I = bd^{3}/3$ (= $bd^{3}/12 + bd\cdot(d/2)^{2}$); about the centroid $bd^{3}/12$.

stem: A rectangle of width $b$ and depth $d$ has centroidal second moment of area about an axis parallel to $b$ equal to:
reason: Centroidal $I$ of a rectangle about the axis parallel to $b$ $= bd^{3}/12$.

stem: For a triangle of base $b$ and height $h$, the second moment of area about the base is:
reason: Triangle: about its base $bh^{3}/12$, about the centroid $bh^{3}/36$, about the apex $bh^{3}/4$.

stem: The second moment of area of a semicircle of diameter $D$ about its diameter is:
reason: Semicircle about its diameter = half the circle’s value = $\pi D^{4}/128 = \pi r^{4}/8$.

stem: For a triangle, the ratio of second moment of area about its centroidal axis to that about its parallel base axis is:
reason: $I_G = bh^{3}/36$ and $I_{\text{base}} = bh^{3}/12$, so $I_G : I_{\text{base}} = 1 : 3$.

stem: The second moment of area of a triangle of base $b$ and height $h$ about a centroidal axis parallel to its base is:
reason: Triangle about its centroidal axis parallel to the base: $bh^{3}/36$.

stem: A solid with an equilateral-triangle base and faces converging to its axis:
reason: Triangular base with faces meeting at an apex = triangular pyramid (tetrahedron); a prism keeps a constant cross-section.

stem: ‘Shape made up of uniform triangles’ (NEC capsule key):
reason: Best pick (medium confidence): Key corrected (old key B). Faces that are all equal triangles = regular tetrahedron = triangular pyramid. A prism also has rectangular side faces, so the old key B is wrong. Low priority: solid shapes are not in syllabus 1.4. · Switch: if ‘tetrahedron’ is offered, choose it.

stem: For a plane area, the perpendicular-axis theorem gives:
reason: Perpendicular axis theorem: $I_z = I_x + I_y$ for a plane lamina (e.g. polar MOI of a circle).

stem: In a closed traverse, $\Sigma\text{north}$ latitude exceeds $\Sigma\text{south}$ latitude and $\Sigma\text{west}$ departure exceeds $\Sigma\text{east}$ departure. The closing line back to the start lies in the:
reason: End point is north-west of the start, so the closing line back to the start runs south-east.
note: Some FTEI keys phrase it as the error “lying in the NW quadrant” — same geometry.

stem: The arithmetic check for the height-of-instrument method of levelling is:
reason: $\Sigma\text{BS} - \Sigma\text{FS} = \text{last RL} - \text{first RL}$ (also $= \Sigma\text{Rise} - \Sigma\text{Fall}$ in the rise-and-fall method).

stem: Compared with the rise-and-fall method, the height-of-instrument method of levelling is generally:

options.B: Quicker, but provides fewer arithmetic checks
options.C: Able to detect every intermediate-sight error automatically

reason: HI method is faster with many intermediate sights but checks only BS and FS, not the intermediate sights.

stem: Number of satellites in the US DoD GPS constellation (nominal):
reason: 24 satellites in 6 orbital planes.

stem: Which is NOT a core GIS capability?
reason: Best pick (medium confidence): In the short textbook list of GIS functions (define the map, represent features, retrieve data), ‘transferring data’ is the odd one out. Real GIS software can still import and export data. · Switch: if asked what GIS software can actually do, data transfer is a real capability.

stem: Which is typically an obstacle to chaining but not to ranging?
reason: A river/pond stops the tape but not the line of sight; a building obstructs both.

stem: A line has magnetic bearing 32°00′ and magnetic declination 10°15′ west. Its true bearing is:
reason: True bearing = magnetic − west declination = 32°00′ − 10°15′ = 21°45′.

stem: Contour lines of different elevations can coincide in plan at a:
reason: Contours of different RL meet only at a vertical cliff and cross only at an overhanging cliff.

stem: For a well-conditioned survey triangle, the smallest angle should generally be at least:
reason: Angles of 30°–120° keep errors small; 60° (equilateral) is ideal.

stem: The whole-circle bearings of AB and BC are 146°30′ and 68°30′. The smaller included angle ABC is:
reason: Back bearing of AB = 326°30′; angle ABC = $\text{FB}(\text{BC}) - \text{BB}(\text{AB}) = 68^\circ30' - 326^\circ30' + 360^\circ = 102^\circ$.

stem: With the level midway between two staff stations and equal sight lengths, which errors approximately cancel in the elevation difference?
reason: Equal sight lengths cancel collimation error and the curvature and refraction corrections.

stem: If a zenith circle reads 98°30′30″ on face left, the corresponding face-right reading is:
Geodetic surveying accounts for:
reason: Geodetic survey allows for the earth’s curvature; plane survey ignores it (areas < ≈ 250 km²).

stem: In building valuation, salvage value is the estimated value at the end of useful life:

options.B: As a built-up property without dismantling

reason: Salvage = value at the end of life without dismantling; scrap = value of dismantled material.

stem: The process of estimating the present fair value of a property is called:
reason: Valuation = estimating the present fair (market) value; depreciation is the loss of value.

stem: A sinking fund is accumulated mainly to:

options.D: Replace an asset at the end of its useful life

reason: A sinking fund accumulates instalments to replace the asset when its life ends.

A conventional approximate allowance of binding wire per 100 kg of reinforcement is:

stem: A level-ground embankment has formation width $B$, height $y$ and side slopes $s$ horizontal to 1 vertical. Its cross-sectional area is:
reason: Area = top width × height + two side triangles ($\tfrac{1}{2}\cdot sy\cdot y$ each) $= By + sy^{2}$.

stem: Who is commonly called the father of soil mechanics?
reason: Karl Terzaghi (Erdbaumechanik, 1925) set out the effective-stress principle.

stem: For a well-graded soil, the coefficient of curvature $C_c$ should generally lie between:
reason: Well graded: $C_c = D_{30}^{2}/(D_{10}\cdot D_{60})$ between 1 and 3, together with $C_u \ge4$ (gravel) or ≥ 6 (sand).

stem: The soil uniformity coefficient $C_u$ is:
reason: $C_u = D_{60}/D_{10}$; $C_u = 1$ means a uniform soil.

stem: For well-graded sand in the unified classification, the $C_u$ criterion is:
reason: USCS well-graded sand: $C_u \ge 6$ and $C_c = 1$–3 (gravel: $C_u \ge 4$).

stem: Porosity $n$ and void ratio $e$ are related by:
The dry density $\rho_d$ of soil with bulk density $\rho$ and gravimetric water content $w$ is:
reason: $\rho_d = \rho/(1 + w)$, with $w$ as a decimal.

stem: The ratio of water volume to void volume in a soil mass is:
reason: $S = V_w/V_v$; porosity $n = V_v/V$; void ratio $e = V_v/V_s$.

stem: A fine-grained inorganic soil plotting below the A-line on the plasticity chart is generally classified as:
reason: Below the A-line → silts (M) and organic soils (O); above → clays (C).

stem: For fully saturated soil with $G_s = 2.6$ and water content $w = 45\%$, porosity is approximately:
Gravimetric water content of soil is:

options.A: Mass of water / mass of dry solids
options.B: Volume of water / volume of voids
options.D: Mass of water / total wet mass

reason: $w = W_w/W_s$ — mass of water divided by mass of dry solids.

stem: In the Unified Soil Classification System, SC denotes:
reason: SC = clayey sand; SM = silty sand; $\text{CL}/\text{CH}$ = clays.

stem: The water content below which further drying no longer reduces soil volume is the:
reason: Shrinkage limit: below it, drying removes water without further volume reduction.

stem: The density-bottle method is commonly used to determine the:
reason: The density bottle (pycnometer) gives the specific gravity of soil solids (≈ 2.65 for sand).

stem: A soil has porosity $n = 0.30$, $e_{\max} = 0.92$ and $e_{\min} = 0.35$. Its density index is approximately:
Neutral stress in saturated soil means:
reason: Neutral stress = pore-water pressure $u$, which carries no shear; $\sigma' = \sigma- u$.

stem: The region between two adjacent flow lines in a flow net is a:
reason: The strip between two adjacent flow lines is a flow channel; the drop between equipotentials is the head drop.

stem: For a flow net in homogeneous isotropic soil, seepage per unit width is:
reason: $q = kH\cdot N_f/N_d$ ($N_f$ flow channels, $N_d$ equipotential drops).

stem: In an isotropic soil flow net, flow lines intersect equipotential lines at:
reason: In an isotropic soil flow lines cut equipotentials at right angles (curvilinear squares).

stem: If a water table already above the ground surface rises further under hydrostatic conditions, the effective stress at a fixed point in the saturated soil:

options.A: Increases by the total water pressure

reason: Extra standing water raises total stress and pore pressure equally, so $\sigma' = \sigma- u$ is unchanged.

stem: A saturated soil has void ratio $e = 0.68$ and specific gravity $G_s = 2.68$. Its critical hydraulic gradient is:
Compaction of a partially saturated soil chiefly reduces its volume by expelling:
reason: Compaction expels air (quick, mechanical); consolidation expels water (time-dependent).

stem: The falling-head permeability test is generally preferred for:
reason: Constant head → sand and gravel; falling head → silts and other low-permeability soils.

stem: Relative compaction is the ratio of:

options.A: Field dry density to specified laboratory maximum dry density
options.B: Field wet density to water density

reason: Relative compaction = field dry density ÷ laboratory maximum dry density (Proctor) × 100.

stem: The coefficient of volume compressibility $m_v$ is the ratio of:
reason: $m_v$ = volumetric strain per unit stress increase = $a_v/(1 + e_0)$.

stem: For saturated clay analysed under the ideal undrained condition $\phi_u = 0$, shear strength is governed by:
reason: $\phi_u = 0$, so $\tau_f = c_u$ (cohesion only); UCC gives $q_u = 2c_u$.

stem: Shear strength of saturated clay is quickly found by:
reason: $c_u = q_u/2$. · Depends on: quick estimate for intact saturated clay; fissured or sensitive clay can mislead.

stem: A cohesionless dry soil fails in triaxial compression at cell pressure 150 kPa and deviator stress 100 kPa. Its friction angle is approximately:
For a dry cohesionless infinite slope with $\phi= 36^\circ$ and factor of safety 1.5, the slope angle $\beta$ is approximately:
reason: $F = \tan\phi/\tan\beta$ → $\tan\beta= \tan36^\circ/1.5 = 0.484$ → $\beta\approx25.8^\circ$.

stem: The field vane-shear test is most suitable for:
reason: The field vane gives in-situ undrained strength of soft, sensitive saturated clay.

stem: Which is correct?

options.D: Failure plane does NOT carry maximum shear stress

reason: Max shear on 45° plane; failure at $45^\circ+ \phi/2$. · Depends on: soil with $\phi> 0$; if $\phi= 0$ the two planes coincide.

stem: Which foundation type is commonly constructed in groups connected by a cap?
reason: Piles are driven in groups and tied by a pile cap that spreads the column load.

stem: Which of the following is a shallow foundation?
reason: Mat/raft is shallow $(D_f \le B)$; caissons and piles are deep foundations.

stem: A pile foundation is ordinarily classified as a:
reason: Piles, piers and wells (caissons) are deep foundations.

stem: Which is NOT a common type of mat foundation?
reason: Types: flat plate, thickened under columns, beam-slab, box, mat on piles. · Depends on: not a standard named mat type; box and piled rafts are.

stem: A mat foundation is adopted when:

options.B: Isolated footings would cover > 50% of area

reason: A mat suits heavy loads on weak soil, especially where isolated footings would cover more than half the plan area. · Depends on: the 50%-coverage rule is economic, not a strict limit.

stem: Minimum depth of a footing below ground (IS 1904):
reason: IS 1904: at least 0.5 m below natural ground, to reach firm soil below seasonal moisture change. · Depends on: general minimum; frost, scour or swelling soil may need more depth.

stem: A single footing that supports two or more columns is generally called a:
reason: A combined footing carries two or more columns, e.g. when their footings would overlap.

stem: A combined footing supporting unequal column loads is often made trapezoidal mainly to:

options.B: Align its area centroid with the load resultant
options.D: Make both columns carry equal loads

reason: The trapezoid’s centroid is moved toward the heavier column so it coincides with the load resultant (uniform pressure).

stem: In Terzaghi’s classical expression for a square footing, ultimate bearing capacity is:
reason: Terzaghi: strip $cN_c + qN_q + 0.5\gamma BN_\gamma$; square $1.3cN_c + qN_q + 0.4\gamma BN_\gamma$; circle uses $0.3\gamma BN_\gamma$.

stem: In Terzaghi’s theory, the elastic wedge under a rough footing makes an angle with the horizontal of:
reason: Terzaghi’s rough base: the elastic wedge faces make $\phi$ with the horizontal; $45^\circ+ \phi/2$ is for a smooth base.

stem: Which is NOT an assumption of Terzaghi’s bearing-capacity theory?
reason: Terzaghi assumes a ROUGH base.

stem: A soil that has previously experienced an effective stress greater than its present effective stress is:
reason: Over-consolidated: past maximum effective stress > present (OCR > 1); it settles less.

stem: Ultimate bearing capacity of a strip on purely cohesive soil (Terzaghi):
reason: $N_c = 5.7$, $N_q = 1$, $N_\gamma = 0$; Skempton $N_c = 5.14$.

stem: Safe bearing capacity of soft rock (IS 1904 table):
reason: Hard rock 3240; laminated rock 1620; shattered rock/hard shale 880; soft rock 440. · Depends on: presumptive table value; the real rock must be checked on site.

stem: Water table has no effect on bearing capacity if it lies below the base of footing at a depth ≥
reason: $R_{w2} = 1$ when $D_w \ge B$ below base. · Depends on: usual correction rule; the real influence depth can differ.

stem: The modulus (coefficient) of subgrade reaction does NOT depend on:
reason: Best pick (low confidence): Mark D (the key): size, shape and depth are the usual corrections for the subgrade modulus k. In the field the water table also changes k, so the claim is not fully true. · Switch: if asked what affects soil support in the field, the water table does matter.

stem: Bearing capacity depends on:
reason: Bearing capacity depends on the soil ($c$, $\phi$, $\gamma$), the footing’s size, shape and depth, and the water table.

stem: An oedometer test primarily measures:
reason: Oedometer = consolidometer: one-dimensional consolidation with lateral strain prevented ($C_c$, $m_v$, $c_v$).

stem: The ratio of consolidation settlement at time $t$ to the ultimate consolidation settlement is called:
reason: Degree of consolidation $U = S_t/S_{\text{final}}$; the time factor is $T_v = c_v\cdot t/d^{2}$.

stem: The gradual reduction in saturated soil volume caused by expulsion of pore water under sustained loading is:
reason: Consolidation = gradual volume decrease from expulsion of pore water under sustained load.

stem: A shallow footing on dense sand or stiff soil most commonly fails by:
reason: Dense sand or stiff clay → general shear; medium → local shear; loose → punching shear.

stem: A shallow footing on sand of medium relative density is more likely to show:

options.A: General shear failure with pronounced heave

reason: Medium-dense sand → local shear failure (partly developed failure surface).

stem: For a soap bubble of radius $R$ and surface tension $T$, the excess internal pressure is:
reason: A soap bubble has two surfaces: $\Delta p = 4T/R = 8T/d$ (droplet $2T/R$).

stem: At approximately what temperature is the density of pure water maximum?
reason: Water is densest (1000 kg/m³) at 4 °C.

stem: Specific volume is the reciprocal of:
reason: Specific volume = volume per unit mass = $1/\rho$ (m³/kg).

stem: Small liquid drops tend to become spherical mainly because of:
reason: Surface tension minimises surface area → spherical drops.

stem: Bulk modulus of a liquid:
reason: $K = 1/\text{compressibility}$. · Depends on: generally true for liquids; it also depends on temperature.

stem: Least compressible among:
reason: Liquids are far less compressible than gases; water’s bulk modulus is about 2.2 GPa.

stem: For the same liquid, contact angle and temperature, the magnitude of capillary rise or depression varies inversely with the tube’s:
reason: $h = 4\sigma\cos\theta/(\rho gd)$ — inversely proportional to the inner radius/diameter.

stem: A Newtonian fluid has shear stress directly proportional to:
reason: Newtonian fluid: $\tau= \mu\cdot du/dy$ (shear stress ∝ velocity gradient).

stem: Three liquids at the same temperature have vapour pressures $V_1 > V_2 > V_3$. Under the same declining external pressure, which starts boiling first?
reason: Highest vapour pressure → most volatile → boils first as pressure falls.

stem: Capillary rise in a wetting liquid is primarily due to:
reason: Capillarity comes from surface tension plus adhesion (wetting) at the liquid–solid contact.

stem: For a given capillary tube and wetting liquid, capillary rise generally does what as temperature increases?
reason: Surface tension falls as temperature rises, so capillary rise decreases.

stem: Viscosity is the property of a fluid that resists:

options.D: Relative motion between adjacent fluid layers

reason: Viscosity resists relative motion (shear) between adjacent layers: $\tau= \mu du/dy$.

stem: For most ordinary liquids, dynamic viscosity with increasing temperature generally:
reason: Liquid viscosity falls with temperature (weaker cohesion); gas viscosity rises.

stem: A point 1 m below a free water surface has gauge pressure approximately:
reason: $p = \rho gh = 1000 \times9.81 \times1 = 9810$ Pa.

stem: In a connected static liquid of uniform density, piezometric head $z + p/\gamma$ is:
reason: In a static fluid $z + p/\gamma$ (piezometric head) is the same everywhere.

stem: Which pressure relation is correct?
reason: $p_{\text{abs}} = p_{\text{atm}} + p_{\text{gauge}}$; vacuum = $p_{\text{atm}} - p_{\text{abs}}$.

stem: A floating body is initially stable for small angular displacements when the metacentre is:

options.C: At the bottom of the body
options.D: Always below the centre of buoyancy

reason: Stable when metacentre $M$ is above $G$ ($GM > 0$); $M$ below $G$ → unstable.

stem: Buoyant force on an immersed body equals the:

options.A: Body’s dry weight in every case

reason: Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced, acting at the centre of buoyancy.

stem: A manometer is used to measure:
reason: Manometers measure pressure or a pressure difference using a liquid column.

stem: Each term in Bernoulli’s head equation $p/\gamma+ V^{2}/(2g) + z$ represents energy per unit:
reason: Bernoulli terms are heads (m) = energy per unit weight.

stem: A jet of area $A$ and velocity $V$ strikes a stationary plate normally and loses its velocity component normal to the plate. The force is:
reason: $F = \rho AV(V - 0) = \rho AV^{2}$ for a stationary plate normal to the jet.

stem: Bernoulli’s equation for ideal steady flow along a streamline expresses conservation of:
reason: Bernoulli expresses conservation of mechanical energy along a streamline (ideal, steady, incompressible).

stem: For an incompressible flow with velocity vector $V$, continuity requires:
reason: Incompressible continuity: $\nabla\cdot V = \partial u/\partial x + \partial v/\partial y + \partial w/\partial z = 0$.

stem: Two identical pipes of diameter $d$ each carry velocity $V$ into one pipe. If the outlet velocity is $2V$, its diameter $D$ is:

stem: Which is NOT a regulatory function of the Nepal Engineering Council?
